title: Quantum codes in the Lee metric
authors: Jinkang Guo, Yiqiu Han, Aranya Chakraborty, Shubham P. Jain, Tianhao Liu, Victor V. Albert, Andrew Lucas
abstract: We introduce a quantum coding framework for discrete small-shift noise, in which errors on qudits are modeled as low-weight $X$- and $Z$-type Pauli shifts, analogous to small phase-space displacements in continuous-variable systems. This structure is approximately respected by nuclear-spin noise and captured by the Lee metric, motivating a quantum extension of classical Lee-metric coding theory. We develop such a formalism for stabilizer codes over $\mathbb{Z}_q$ for arbitrary $q$, using joint and separate Lee metrics for the $X$- and $Z$-components of errors. For qubits, the joint metric counts $Y$ errors twice and can yield codes that detect and correct $X$ and $Z$ errors with fewer physical qubits than codes designed for the conventional Hamming metric. We discuss Lee-weight spreading under Clifford gates and qubitize codes over $\mathbb{Z}_4$ via the Gray map, finding codes with two-fold transversal non-qubit-Clifford gates. For quantum CSS Lee-LDPC codes on $n$ qudits, we prove that the Lee distance cannot exceed $O(n)$, uniformly in $q$, demonstrating an unexpected obstruction to using the large internal Hilbert space of a large-$q$ qudit to make high-Lee-distance codes. Under local Metropolis dynamics, certain classical $q$-ary ``helical repetition codes'' have exponentially long memory times at fixed temperature for sufficiently large $q$ (that grows with system length), which can be understood as spontaneous symmetry breaking at finite temperature, even in local one-dimensional models. Hypergraph products of these helical repetition codes provide local two-dimensional quantum codes that inherit self-correction for $Z$ errors, but self-correction for $X$ errors remains an open question.
summary: This paper introduces a quantum coding theory framework for qudits designed to combat discrete small-shift noise, utilizing the Lee metric instead of the standard Hamming metric. It develops mathematical tools to analyze stabilizer codes under this metric, showing potential advantages in qubit count and establishing fundamental bounds on achievable code distances. The work advances the theory of fault-tolerant quantum computation by incorporating realistic noise models.
main_problem: The paper develops a quantum coding framework to address noise modeled by discrete small-shift Pauli errors (X and Z shifts) in qudit systems, moving beyond standard assumptions of equally likely errors.
main_result: It establishes that the joint Lee metric can yield qubit codes with fewer physical qubits than Hamming metric codes, and it proves an obstruction showing the Lee distance for qudit LDPC codes is bounded by $O(n)$.
method: The authors develop a formalism for stabilizer codes over $\mathbb{Z}_q$ using joint and separate Lee metrics, analyzing error spreading under Clifford gates and employing techniques like the Gray map for qubitization.
model_or_system: The system involves qudits (systems with $q$ levels) subjected to noise modeled by low-weight X- and Z-type Pauli shifts. The theoretical framework is built around generalizing classical Lee-metric coding theory to the quantum domain.
key_observables: Lee distance, code distance, error spread ($	ext{w}_B(U)$), and memory times for classical codes.
important_parameters: The qudit dimension $q$, the system size $n$, and the temperature $T$ (for classical dynamics).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the noise structure is governed by the Lee metric, which weights errors based on the total size of X and Z shifts, rather than assuming all Pauli shifts are equally likely.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the Lee metric for qudits, develops the formalism for stabilizer codes using joint/separate metrics, analyzes specific constructions (e.g., qubitization, LDPC codes), and concludes with discussions on classical analogues and open questions.
why_interesting: The work directly tackles advanced topics in quantum error correction by incorporating a physically motivated, non-uniform error model (the Lee metric) into the theory of qudit codes, which is highly relevant to understanding realistic noise in quantum hardware.

Figure 2: Two Lee metrics on Pauli errors. Each cell of the 5 × 5 grid is the single-qudit Pauli error XaZb with a, b ∈{−2, −1, 0, 1, 2} (q ≥5). (a) The separate metric assigns to XaZb the pair (|a|L, |b|L), and the errors with both entries at most t form a square of side length 2t + 1. (b) The joint metric (2.6) assigns the single number |a|L + |b|L, and the errors of joint Lee weight at most t form a Lee ball of radius t. For q ≥2t + 1, the Lee ball is a polyomino with 2t2 + 2t + 1 cells that approximates a rhombus [49]. For t = 1, it is the plus-shaped pentomino. Figure 3: Checks of the lifted-Hamming toric code. One Zq qudit sits on each edge, and the number on an edge is the exponent of the Pauli operator applied to it, with λ a root of λ2 −λ + 2 in Zq as in Example 4.9. (a) The X check at a vertex (dot) applies X1, Xλ, Xλ−1, X−1 along four edges to the east and four edges to the south. (b) The Z check at a plaquette corner (dot) applies the same exponents to four horizontal edges to the north and the negated exponents to four vertical edges to the west, in the row just below the dot. Every check occupies the dashed 4 × 4 window, for every q.

Figure 4: Numerically estimated mean hitting time of the PBC helical repetition code HPBC(2, −1) as a function of q = 2n −1 at different inverse temperatures β. Starting from the all-zero codeword, we evolve the system under the Monte Carlo Metropolis algorithm and record the first time when the state becomes closer, in Lee distance, to the neighboring codeword v = (1, 2, . . . , 2n−1) than to the initial codeword. The data are plotted on a semilog scale, with a logarithmic vertical axis.

Figure 5: Local Tanner-graph schematic for the mixed helical HGP code built from the horizontal PBC (ah, −bh) helical code and the vertical OBC (av, −bv) helical code. Filled and open circles denote the two types of physical qudits in the HGP code. We label the filled-circle qudits by pairs (r, i), with i ∈Z/nZ and r = 1, . . . , n, and label the open-circle qudits by pairs (b, i), with i ∈Z/nZ and b = 1, . . . , n −1. The coordinate i is periodic in the horizontal direction, while r labels positions in the open vertical direction. Squares denote X-checks, and diamonds denote Z-checks.
